result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of the victor statues at Olympia, naming athletes and their sculptors. He disputes the identity of the Gelon who dedicated a chariot, and tells how the boxer Cleomedes of Astypalæa went mad, vanished into a chest and was honoured as a hero.

scenes.title: Statues of boy and men victors
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists statues of Theognetus, Xenocles, Alcetus, Aristeus, Chimon and Philles with their sculptors. He notes the story of Taurosthenes' apparition at Ægina.

scenes.title: Which Gelon dedicated the chariot?
scenes.summary: Pausanias argues from the inscription and the dates that the dedicator was Gelon of Gela, not the Syracusan tyrant. Glaucias made the chariot and statue.

scenes.title: Cleomedes of Astypalæa
scenes.summary: Cleomedes kills Iccus in a boxing match, is denied the prize and goes mad, then collapses a school roof. He hides in a chest in Athene's temple and vanishes; Delphi orders him honoured as a hero.
scenes.stakes: Cleomedes faces death by stoning from the citizens after killing the schoolboys.

scenes.title: Philo and Agametor
scenes.summary: Pausanias mentions the statue of Philo with Simonides' couplet, and that of Agametor.

notable_quotes.reason: The Delphic oracle declares Cleomedes the last of the heroes, to be worshipped as no longer mortal.

analysis.text: Pausanias catalogues statues but digresses into local legends and critical checks, showing his blend of guidebook and antiquarian scholarship.
The Cleomedes story reflects Greek hero cult, in which exceptional or disappearing figures could be honoured as heroes on Delphi's advice.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias corrects earlier writers by comparing the inscription with Olympiad and Athenian archon dates.

language_notes.text: Pausanias admits he cannot explain why the statue holds pine fruit (a cone) and pomegranate, and guesses at a local Æginetan legend.
The first man is unnamed; Elis did not register him because his victory came in the trotting-race (a mule-cart event), which was later abolished.
The temple of Peace in Rome was built by Vespasian and housed many Greek artworks taken from Greece.
The apparition is a double: Taurosthenes' likeness appeared at Ægina the same day, announcing his Olympic victory far away.
Dating by the Athenian Archon and Olympiad year was the standard way to fix events; Pausanias uses it to prove his chronology.
Umpires translates the Olympic judges (Hellanodicae), who could strip a victor of his prize for a foul.
The oracle declares Cleomedes the last of the heroes, meaning he is to be worshipped as a demigod rather than mourned as a man.

context_notes.text: Gelon, tyrant of Syracuse, was a famous Sicilian ruler who defeated the Carthaginians; Pausanias distinguishes him from a namesake of Gela.
The Pythian Priestess was the priestess of Apollo at Delphi, whose oracles settled questions of cult and honours.
Simonides of Ceos was a celebrated lyric poet who wrote many epigrams for victors' statues.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias presents himself as a critical historian who weighs evidence and corrects earlier writers.
Pausanias distances himself from the tale with 'they say', reporting local tradition while building a vivid, escalating story of grief and madness.
The searchers break open the chest and find it empty, a striking reversal of what a hiding man should leave behind.
